title: The New Blocs of 2026: Who Is Lining Up With Whom
description:
In 2002 a US president named an "axis of evil". In 2026 the world is splitting into blocs again, but not along the old lines. Russia and North Korea have a mutual defence treaty. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey have just signed one of their own. NATO has grown. And India sits in groups on both sides. Here is the map of who is lining up with whom, and what these pacts actually promise.

Facts as reported up to 1 November 2026 (sources below). The words "axis" and "bloc" are the labels others use, not formal alliances, except where a treaty is named.

Maps: country borders as shown by the Survey of India (Natural Earth, India view). Satellite imagery: NASA Blue Marble; contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025-2026.
core_message: New pacts are redrawing the map in 2026, and India is one of the few countries with a seat in rival groups.
comment_question: Should India pick a side, or keep a seat in every group?

scenes.narration: In January 2002, President George W. Bush named three countries an axis of evil: Iran, Iraq and North Korea.
scenes.heading: 2002: the "axis of evil"

scenes.narration: It was never an alliance. The three had no treaty binding them together. It was a label.
Twenty-four years later, the world really is splitting into blocs. But they are new ones, with real treaties, and some surprising members.
So who is lining up with whom? And what do these pacts actually promise?
Start with the group some analysts call the axis of upheaval: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.
scenes.heading: The "axis of upheaval"

scenes.narration: The name comes from analysts at the Center for a New American Security in Washington. These four countries have no single treaty. What they have is a web of deals.
scenes.text: Not one treaty, a web of deals

scenes.narration: The strongest link is between Moscow and Pyongyang. In June 2024 they signed a treaty that commits each to help the other if it is attacked.
scenes.heading: Russia and North Korea: a defence treaty

scenes.narration: North Korea has since sent ammunition, missiles and thousands of troops, who fought for Russia in its Kursk region.
scenes.heading: North Korean troops in Kursk

scenes.narration: Iran supplied Russia with drones early in the war in Ukraine. Russia has since built its own versions at home.
scenes.text: Iranian drones, now made in Russia

scenes.narration: But Russia and Iran's own treaty, signed in January 2025, has no mutual defence clause. When the United States and Israel struck Iran this year, Russia did not go to war for it.
scenes.text: No promise to defend each other

scenes.narration: And China is the biggest member by far. It buys large volumes of Russian oil and has helped it get around Western sanctions on chips and components, analysts say. But it has no defence pact with any of the other three except a decades-old treaty with North Korea.
scenes.heading: China: the biggest, and the most careful

scenes.narration: China's treaty with North Korea dates from 1961, and it is the only one China has that promises military help.
scenes.text: China's only defence treaty: North Korea, 1961

scenes.narration: So this isn't a NATO of the East. It's a set of partners who help each other where it suits them.
Now a newer bloc, much closer to India. On the seventh of August 2026, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
scenes.heading: The Mecca pact

scenes.narration: Its core promise is that any armed attack against one of the three shall be regarded as an attack against them all.
scenes.text: Any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all.
scenes.author: Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, 7 August 2026

scenes.narration: That sounds like NATO's Article five. Under this pact, though, each country decides for itself what help to send.
scenes.text: Each member decides its own help

scenes.narration: It grew out of a pact Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed in Riyadh in September 2025. Turkey joined, and the three met in Mecca to make it bigger.
scenes.heading: From Riyadh to Mecca

scenes.narration: In October, the three agreed to deploy forces to Saudi Arabia to counter Houthi attacks, and Turkey sent the agreement to its parliament for ratification.
Others may join. Turkey wants Egypt in. Syria said it was considering it, and Bangladesh said it was positive about a future framework.
India's foreign ministry said it values its partnership with Saudi Arabia and expects Riyadh to keep India's interests and sensitivities in mind.
Analysts doubt the pact puts Saudi Arabia or Turkey under Pakistan's nuclear umbrella. But it does tie a nuclear-armed neighbour of India to two of the Muslim world's biggest powers.
scenes.text: A nuclear power in the pact

scenes.narration: On the other side, the Western alliance has grown. Finland joined NATO in 2023 and Sweden in 2024. Finland alone more than doubled the alliance's land border with Russia.
scenes.heading: NATO grows north

scenes.narration: In Asia, the United States leans on treaties with Japan, South Korea, the Philippines and Australia.
scenes.heading: America's Pacific allies

scenes.narration: Even this side is not one bloc. Washington has pushed its allies to pay more, and in 2025 NATO members agreed to aim for five percent of their economies on defence and security by 2035.
And that's the pattern everywhere. Fewer permanent camps, more deals for a single purpose.
Which brings us to India. India is a member of the Quad, with the United States, Japan and Australia.
scenes.heading: India in the Quad

scenes.narration: It is also a founding member of BRICS, with Brazil, Russia, China and South Africa, a group that has grown to take in Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia, the UAE and Indonesia.
scenes.heading: India in BRICS

scenes.narration: It buys Russian oil, trades with Gulf states, and has ships allowed through Hormuz by Iran while it holds naval exercises with the United States in the Indian Ocean.
India calls this strategic autonomy. It has no mutual defence treaty with anyone.
The question for the next few years is whether that still works when the blocs around it harden.
So what to watch? Whether Egypt or others join the Mecca pact. Whether North Korean troops stay in Russia. And whether the end of the Iran war pulls these blocs closer, or pushes them apart.
scenes.heading: What to watch
items: Do North Korean troops stay in Russia?
Does the Iran war's end pull blocs together or apart?

scenes.narration: In 2002, an axis was a label. In 2026, the lines on this map are being written into treaties.
scenes.heading: Lines written into treaties

scenes.narration: Should India pick a side, or keep a seat in every group? Tell us what you think in the comments.
scenes.text: Pick a side, or keep every seat?
